content: Adenoidectomy, which involves the surgical removal of the adenoids, is a widely performed procedure in children who experience recurrent or chronic nasal symptoms. However, a systematic review specifically evaluating the effectiveness of adenoidectomy in this group of children has not been conducted previously. The objective of this review was to determine whether adenoidectomy is more effective than non-surgical management in treating children with recurrent or chronic nasal symptoms. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Ear, Nose and Throat Disorders Group Trials Register, CENTRAL, PubMed, EMBASE, CINAHL, Web of Science, BIOSIS Previews, Cambridge Scientific Abstracts, and mRCT. Both published and unpublished trials were considered, with the most recent search completed on March 30, 2009. The inclusion criteria for the review were randomized controlled trials that compared adenoidectomy (with or without tympanostomy tubes) to non-surgical management or tympanostomy tubes alone in children with recurrent or chronic nasal symptoms. The primary outcomes assessed included the frequency of episodes, the duration of each episode, the total number of symptomatic days per year, and the proportion of children experiencing recurrent nasal symptoms. Secondary outcomes included the average number of episodes, the average duration of each episode, the total number of symptomatic days per year, and the proportion of children with nasal obstruction as the sole symptom. Two independent authors evaluated the quality of the trials and extracted the relevant data. However, only one study specifically included children undergoing adenoidectomy for recurrent or chronic nasal symptoms or middle ear disease. This study, which involved 76 participants, did not demonstrate any significant benefit of adenoidectomy. The quality of the study was moderate, and the sample size was small. The primary outcome measured was the improvement in episodes of common colds. The risk differences were not statistically significant, with values of 2% (95% confidence interval [CI]: -18% to 22%) at 12 months and -11% (95% CI: -28% to 7%) at 24 months. A second study included 180 children with recurrent acute otitis media, a condition often associated with nasal symptoms. In this study, the number of days with rhinitis was analyzed as a secondary outcome. Again, the results were not statistically significant, with a risk difference of -4 days (95% CI: -13 to 7 days). The authors concluded that the current evidence regarding the effectiveness of adenoidectomy in managing recurrent or chronic nasal symptoms, or nasal obstruction alone, is limited, inconclusive, and subject to a high risk of bias. They emphasized the need for high-quality randomized controlled trials to better assess the efficacy of adenoidectomy in this population.
